I really thought Spike Lee was joking with this one. No way this could be an anti-racist film like some critics are arguing. This is precisely what a hateful racist film looks like. The way black people are portrayed is stereotypical, and that's surprising. I'm not sure if this is only obvious for people who do not live in the States. Any white critic who says this film is impressive is only because they are too afraid to sound racist. Everyone is trying to sound politically correct and use the word "ethical" as a cookie cutter tool to look at everything around them. A critic should not be afraid to talk about anything, let alone being afraid to be "offensive." It's absolutely preposterous that people think about being offensive. And because of this everyone is self-censoring themselves. I read from some critics that Green Book was a racist film made by a white person when compared to this film which was anti-racist made by an "intellectual" director. I did not feel that way at all. I think white critics are too afraid of their own racist thoughts, so they search for anything that resembles their own opinions. They feel like they have to love anti-racist films made by oppressed people even if the film (or any artwork for that matter) is terrible. And yes, this film is awful. Editing is a joke, the floating heads in the dark during Kwame's speech was laughable with calls and cries that sound like they were being said by a white person trying to sound black. How did anyone keep a straight face making this film? If they thought this film was serious, then they were accepting Spike Lee's discriminative and derogatory way. I hope people start making overly-offensive films so maybe some of those people who are all PC could wake up well healed after going into a coma watching them.

Really good as a film that was made with technique and ability. But tons of negative points for: - the “not all cops are bad” codedness that ultimately completely ignores the real role police have in our society as well as the systemic nature to these conflicts - The liberal misrepresentation of radical, anticapitalist black liberation movements of the decades as an aesthetic (but yea the aesthetic is cool…) - the framing of Stallworth as a good cop hero who disrupted the KKK to applause from his good white cop friends; he was mostly IRL a plant for disruption to Marxist liberation groups… It’s just so hilarious to show white cops joining in on catching the one overtly racist cop. In the 19 fucking 70s. Oh my god shut up racism is not this individualized caricature of singular bad guys, and I guarantee every actual cop in Colorado Springs in the 70s was just as racist as Felix. AND conservatives today are just as racist as him despite how polite they may act to your face sometimes! They aren’t all actually David duke, most of them are your families and friends who smile and shake your hand then vote your rights away, cheering on the billionaires poisoning your poor neighbor’s water and posting 15 Facebook posts a day about how immigrants are criminals and “he should’ve just listened to the cop’s orders”

The more I think about this movie, and everything that is wrong with it, the more it upsets me. As a story, it fails to be compelling, interesting, or sensical, and as a political message, I am left speechless in how badly it falls short and wastes it potential. Not to be dramatic, but the overall positive reception it has received makes me feel like white film viewers praise Spike Lee's conversations about race because they genuinely do not understand the intricacies at play, while black film viewers give him a pass due to the lack of black directors within mainstream American cinema. I'm genuinely disappointed.

Instead of the movie being about Black people, it became a movie about a Jew and the holocaust somehow! Not to mention that the movie is a straight up copaganda.

absolutely not. i thought this movie would be about a black man befriending klan members outside of the klan and showing them black people’s humanity and ultimately making them voluntarily quit the klan, because i had read an article about something like that actually happening and i thought that was an interesting story. that story would have been much better. wtf is this. apparently this is a real story but i’m incredulous because it’s so unnecessarily complicating things to have a black man lead the undercover cop investigation into the klan since he’d never be accepted as an actual member which is a requirement to do undercover stuff smoothly. also the investigation was meaningless and i was confused what the goal was because it wasn’t like they were even trying to disband the group. it just seemed like something white liberals would do as a joke or sth to make fun of their racist rhetoric, not an actual cop investigation. like ha ha david duke talked to a black man whom he thought was a white man ha ha ha? it’s not that funny. also, it’s obviously copaganda. why are we even focusing on a black cop who at the beginning of the movie went undercover to a black power speech? baffling why he couldn’t see patrice’s defiance against cops as valid when he literally spied on them to gather intel for the cops. the police has been a racist institution without a doubt and the klan could lynch and do extremely violent stuff to black people precisely because the cops backed them and didn’t punish them for their violent crusades. they definitely enabled the klan, so where was the reflection on that. i was way more interested in hearing what kwame ture had to say and patrice’s life story than a black man working as a lap dog for the police spying on his own “brothers and sisters”. like i get that this movie wanted to disavow white supremacy and equate the kkk with charlottesville and trump in the year 2018. okay. if you want to be anti racist, is showing members of the kkk extensively really the best way to achieve that goal? i wish this movie had been about the black panther movement and people like patrice, not this. baffling “true” story told in an even more baffling and frustrating manner to achieve nothing.

I would like to start off by saying that as someone who really loved Do the Right Thing I was very excited to watch this movie. I mean, who wouldn't after reading that premise right? The sheer concept of a black cop infiltrating the KKK immediately got my attention...yet this film almost completely falls apart on every level. The first and last 5 minutes are great. The last scene with Ron and Patrice especially actually had me lock tf in, that was a powerful way to wrap the story up in a way I never expected. Everything else is kinda ass. I just wanna say that the editing in this movie is unironically one of the worst I've seen. The shots have absolutely no continuity after cutting, it keeps cutting in the most awkward moments, the genuinely powerful speech at the beginning has some really goofy closeups of the audience for some reason, there's just endless examples of atrocious editing that made it impossible for me to have fun with the film. This movie should have been a comedy, but for some reason it's a terrible one even with a premise this silly. There's nothing snappy about the intentionally comedic lines, it's just kind of awkwardly lumbering in its own rhythm and it's not funny. The acting is fine but nothing memorable. Adam Driver gave a better performance in Megalopolis of all things than this movie. The social commentary here also is just surface level as hell and cheap. It's genuinely shocking coming from the man behind one of the most nuanced movies on race tensions, that the main thing explored here is white people are racist. Any room for nuance set up by the plot of the movie: Adam Driver wrestling with his Jew heritage, Patrice's, and her people in general, hatred of cops, Ron's weird insistence on believing in changing the system from inside never truly being explored nor challenged, the racist cop(s) in Ron's department, and so much more are just...dropped? They don't reach anywhere close to resolution nor is there any development with these themes, they're just mentioned briefly and discarded. Why does Ron need to be on the phone? Why can't Adam Driver just be on the phone and meeting them in person? The premise itself has holes, and throughout the entire movie I honestly don't know what our characters are doing in the KKK. Do they really learn anything of value? Do I, the audience, even learn anything from watching this movie? There's not even like a comical examination of KKK's weird activities and procedures like I thought they would, it's like there's barely any research done into the organisation you're making a movie about. The whole movie is just Adam Driver and Ron dicking around in the KKK and hearing white people spam hate speech. It's not entertaining, funny, nor educational. It's cheap . The fucking 5 minutes KKK cutscene in Django Unchained with Quentin Tarantino as a racist Klan member was like a thousand times more entertaining than this movie in a fraction of its screentime.

Je ne parviens pas à comprendre le concept de ce film qui est censé dénoncer le racisme, l’antisémitisme et l’homophobie aux Etats-Unis à travers l’histoire vraie d’un policier Noir qui est parvenu à infiltrer le Ku Klux Klan dans les années 70, mais dont la légèreté de ton, voire la nonchalance des personnages, contraste trop avec la gravité du sujet. Cette hésitation dans le traitement du film, entre images d’archives qui font froid dans le dos et scènes comiques à la sauce Starsky et Hutch, noie ainsi le propos dans un mélange des genres qui ne convainc pas. Si l’humour s’avère une arme cinématographique souvent efficace pour dénoncer des actes répréhensibles, il l’est bien plus quand l’intégralité du film repose sur la comédie. Ici, l'ensemble est trop caricatural et Spike Lee semble trop hésiter entre drame, pamphlet et scènes de pure comédie (pas toujours drôles, d’ailleurs), produisant une oscillation contre-productive qui dessert son sujet. Si le projet demeure louable, on est bien loin des fulgurances passées du réalisateur.

What Spike Lee does is present this film as radical critique when it's actually functioning as counterinsurgence. On the surface you get a satisfying story where a Black cop infiltrates and disrupts the Klan. But that completely obscures the actual history that white supremacy wasn't ann external enemy. It was built into law enforcement and governance itself. The real problem is, it's neutralization dressed up as radical filmmaking, which might be worse than just making a bad movie because it makes you think the problem is already solved when it was never actually addressed.

It's always a bit difficult to rate films based on true stories. It raises questions such as : should you aestheticize things that weren't ? Should a film's faithfulness to real events affect its rating ? Does it still need to be entertaining in the way it's directed ? In terms of pure feeling and a basic judgment, I can't help feeling that the film is wasted potential. It's only near the end that it comes close to the level of stress and tension that could have been present throughout the entire film, and it was only when real footage was shown for a few minutes that I felt genuinely hurt and outraged. Going back to the questions I raised at the beginning, I think the film tried too hard to stay entertaining and visually appealing, to the point of becoming almost comical by adding subtle humor to every scene and turning every character into a caricature. Or maybe white supremacists really were that ridiculous back then and I'm the one who's wrong ? But I think it's more likely a huge mistake on Spike Lee's part, combined with mid acting and mid direction. There's a serious lack of raw scenes showing the emotional struggles some of these characters may have gone through. The film almost gives the impression that social segregation wasn't all that violent, that racists were only a minority and that infiltrating a group of dangerous unstable sick individuals is just routine. And after a few quick searches, it becomes clear that the film is far from Ron Stallworth's real story. He first spent three years infiltrating black activists and radical black groups before infiltrating the KKK for nine months, not just one for a night and the other for a month. In conclusion, Spike Lee reduced reality to the story of a somewhat cool black cop infiltrating a group of somewhat stupid racists who do some not so nice things. But on the whole, it’s not a complete disaster with no substance or form. It’s just that looking at the film’s overall rating I get the impression that everyone has kind of agreed it’s a very good movie that represents the cause well. I suppose the intention was there, and the goal was still to highlight an important and underrepresented period of history, so let’s not be too harsh either.

i believe my expectations were set too high for this film. and while i give merit to the aesthetic devices used to make this film, the lighting, cinematography, and music, this film was truly void of revolutionary political commentary or characterization. now, after reading other reviews on here, i understand that this was a complete falsified retelling of the main character’s true story. a man who was actually undercover for three years infiltrating black radical groups with the intention of causing the destabilization and downplay of their work. the writers picked apart and fabricated many parts of his story to make it seem like the main character and the police were fighting against racism. i mean, how inaccurate is this? the police, in rural colorado in the 70s, were working AGAINST the KKK? right. blatant copaganda and assimilation ideation. which makes sense given Spike Lee’s association with the NYPD, where they gave him over 200K for an ad campaign to promote relationships between the police and the black community. the characters seemed completely flat, what was Ron’s backstory? what were his motivations? why did Patrice get actively assaulted by a cop and then have no discussion about it? just a cut to an aestheticized montage. this was truly a disappointment on so many levels, not that we can expect radical media from large media corporations, but the premise seemed interesting while the film slowly descended into nonsense. especially the last scene at the bar with the cringe dialogue and arrest of the racist cop who had assaulted Patrice prior in the film, who was arrested on the grounds of saying racist shit? with that logic the entire KKK could have been rounded up an hour into the movie. painting the cops in a heroic light in a film about black subjugation and white violence is a fucking joke. and ending the film with a memoriam for a white white woman at the hands of white hatred instead of the thousands upon thousands of black and brown people killed by the systemic violence of the police? disgusting and tone deaf.

I promise I’m not racist but wow this was not good. This is my first Spike Lee joint and if his others are like this I will be very disappointed. This film has very strong themes and some great acting from Topher Grace and Adam Driver but the John David Washington felt a bit out of place. The end montage of present day is disturbing and really worked for me. So was most of the third act. But there is a lot of bad… This is the worst editing I have seen from a major film ever. There are a lot of times especially in the epilogue where they’ll be an action done in one shot that will be taken and done again in the second. I don’t know if this is Lee’s style but it felt crazy that this made it into the final cut of the film. The fast cuts felt weird and took me out of the story. The writing in this is very confusing. It’s hard to tell at time if they are being serious or trying to have a comedic moment. I find a lot of this movie boring and a struggle to get through. I hated some of this choices in this movie especially when Ron and Patrice are walking and talking about movies and it popped up with the posters on the screen. That felt way out of the film. Some parts felt very Tarintino and I don’t like that. Have your own style… One day I hope I can rewatch this and like it but right now this is bad.

(The final sequence is really great)

What a rage movie. Spent 80% of the film angry at white supremacists and the other 20% pissed at Ron. Stressed as hell the whole time. Love that they added a fictional Black Student Union member as Ron's love interest just so they could gloss over/excuse his infiltration of the Panthers. Ron can't be part of a racist system... he has sex with Black activists! The Kwame Ture scene was fucking nauseating. Too many scenes juxtaposing White Nationalism with the Black Power movement without any further thoughts for my taste. The ending almost brings it back around but not really. Topher Grace as David Duke was fucking hilarious casting though. Genuinely entertaining film but I'm upset. It has its moments of being quite visually beautiful, compelling, funny... but definitely a "not all cops" film at the end of the day. I really liked Noel Ransome's Vice article on this film, "‘BlacKkKlansman’ Creates a Safe-Space for White Audiences to Trivialize Racism."

The idea is good, but the acting is more bad than good. Adam’s driver is good in this and John is okay. The overdubbed lines are absolutely horrifically awful. The whole film feels so rushed and really not a clear point in pacing. Overall it could be better, if all those things would have been fixed. The whole entirety of the film is great, I love detective movies but it’s all those other things that I listed that just make me not able to see beyond those things. So overall. Good idea, bad execution.
